The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg is the **RMS Titanic**.

To explain the complex concept of blockchain technology using an analogy, imagine a massive, shared notebook that is kept by thousands of people all over the world. In a traditional system, like a bank, only one person (the bank) holds the official notebook and writes down every transaction. If that person makes a mistake or decides to cheat, it’s hard to prove otherwise because you don’t have access to the original record.

In a blockchain system, however, everyone has a copy of this notebook. When a new transaction happens, it’s like writing a new page in the notebook. But here’s the key difference: before that page is added, everyone else checks their own notebooks to make sure the transaction is valid. If the majority agrees that the transaction is legitimate, the new page is added to everyone’s notebook at the same time.

This makes the system "immutable" because once a page is written and agreed upon, it cannot be erased or changed without everyone else noticing and rejecting the change. It is "decentralized" because no single person or company controls the entire book; instead, the power and the record are distributed across all the computers (or people) holding copies. This collective verification process ensures that the data is secure, transparent, and trustworthy, much like a community of witnesses who all agree on what happened.
